newsitem.title: UK: British Conservatives close ranks for election.
newsitem.headline: British Conservatives close ranks for election.

text.p: It is the clearest sign that Britain's general election is just months away: the ruling Conservatives have stopped fighting among themselves.

Driven by an election-winning instinct that lets them boast of being the world's most successful political party, the Conservatives this week restored the unity they need to have any chance of overhauling of Tony Blair's opposition Labour party.
The ceasefire which broke out at their annual party conference may yet prove to be short-lived. Divisions over Europe, and to a lesser extent taxes, remain deep.

But even before Prime Minister John Major sends the party faithful home on Friday with a rallying cry for the election, due by May, Conservative activists and ministers alike say they mean what they say about closing ranks.

"What we should not tolerate is members of our party feeding the voracious appetite of a media anxious to headline any phrase, any whisper, that harms our cause and serves our opponents," Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine said.
"And particularly when they choose to do so at a time of maximum damage to the party. That deserves our contempt."

The conference started on Tuesday under a dark cloud, with allegations of sleaze against a former trade minister rubbing salt in wounds raw from months of infighting over Major's wait-and-see stance toward Europe's planned single currency.

But Margaret Thatcher, no great admirer of Major, her successor as prime minister, set the tone for reconcilation early on by publicly praising him and declaring that a Conservative victory had never been more important.

By Wednesday, the mood in the conference hall was lifting perceptibly as activists swung behind arguments by Major and his foreign secretary, Michael Rifkind, that Britain must not to close off its options on whether to scrap the pound sterling.
Unity in previous years was shattered by virulent speeches on the fringe of the conference by "Euro-sceptics" opposed to closer European ties, notably the single currency set for 1999.

The Euro-sceptics have not suddenly been converted on the road to Brussels. But, facing the real possibiliy of a Labour landslide, big-hitters such as former cabinet ministers John Redwood and Norman Lamont pulled their punches.

"We've had a great argument, but the differences between us are as nothing compared to the differences with the Labour party over Europe," said Lamont -- a far cry from his controversial call at the 1994 conference for Britain to consider leaving the European Union.
Party harmony at previous conferences was also threatened by challenges, perceived or real, to Major's leadership by cabinet ministers jockeying to succeed him.
Such coded messages were conspicuous by their absence this year, replaced by earnest appeals for loyalty.
"One thing that has always marked the Conservative party apart is its will to govern and its determination to win, said Defence Secretary Michael Portillo, one right-wing pretender to Major's crown.
"But I tell this conference: in order to win we need three extra policies -- unity, unity and unity."

The stiffest test of the party's newly-rediscovered unity came when finance minister Kenneth Clarke, a hate figure for right-wingers because of his enthusiasm for a single currency and coolness towards tax cuts, took the stage.
There had been rumours that Clarke, the victim of a whispering campaign, would be barracked. In the event, he won a lengthy standing ovation.

The harmony, Labour critics will say, was predictable. But if it translates into a bounce in the next opinion polls, Tony Blair will know that after months of shadow-boxing he finally has a real fight on his hands.
